subject: Throughput SLO carve-out request and queueing guidance for Reserved-GPU pools
messages:
From: Sophie Tanner <sophie.tanner@nimbus-analytics.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>
Cc: CloudOps Procurement <procure@cloudops.com>
Date: 2026-08-04T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: Dedicated pool throughput and evening spike behavior

Hi Kimberly / Neha —

Thanks again for the call this morning. As we discussed, Nimbus runs a nightly enrichment pipeline between 02:00–05:00 PT that bursts to ~6–8x our daytime token rate for short windows (10–30 minutes). We want to move from a hosted shared plan to a reserved GPU pool but need clarity on two things before procurement will sign:

1) Exact throughput SLOs you can commit to at the per-GPU level and what queueing behavior looks like when the pool hits saturation. We need to understand tail latency and whether shorter requests (seq len ~128) still see acceptable p95/p99 under heavy queue depth.

2) Contract language / credits: how do you calculate SLA credits for throughput violations vs. pure availability? Procurement prefers a clear credit formula (e.g., % credits per 1% below agreed throughput for >5 consecutive minutes).

I've attached a short doc with our procurement requirements and a rough expected load shape. Can you confirm if Redwood can support: 1) a dedicated 8x-A100-equivalent pool with an ingress SLO of 3k tokens/s baseline and 6k tokens/s burst for up to 20 minutes, and 2) either a priority queue for enrichment jobs or guaranteed headroom so burst jobs don't starve interactive traffic?

Appreciate a short note on feasible options and we'll route to our legal/procurement.

Best,
Sophie
[Attachment: procurement_requirements.docx (docx, 52KB)]

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>
To: Sophie Tanner <sophie.tanner@nimbus-analytics.com>
Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-08-04T13:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated pool throughput and evening spike behavior

Hi Sophie — thanks for the clear summary and the procurement doc. High level answers up front: yes, we can support a dedicated pool with firm throughput targets, but the commercial and technical approach depends on the isolation level you want during bursts. Two viable patterns: 

Option A — Dedicated baseline + burst credits (recommended for most customers)\- You reserve an 8-GPU pool (A100 equivalent). Guarantee: baseline sustained throughput of 3k tokens/s across the pool with p95 latency <120ms for seq len 128 and p99 < 350ms.\- Burst: additional pooled capacity in the same tenancy (burst credits) that allows you to spike to 6k tokens/s for up to 20 minutes. During burst, we apply a short-term fair-share policy so interactive traffic retains a minimum latency floor.

Option B — Strict throughput carve-out (hard reservation)\- We dedicate a set of GPUs exclusively to your workload; we guarantee up to 6k tokens/s for bursts but require a minimum contract uplift (typically 1.5x committed baseline) to assure headroom. This gives deterministic queueing (FIFO within your tenant) but is more expensive.

Queueing behavior notes:\- Our default priority model is: interactive (low-latency) > scheduled batch (enrichment) > background. We can create a two-tier queue for you: priority queue for interactive calls and a preemptible batch queue for enrichment. Preemptible batch jobs may be throttled or delayed during sustained high interactive traffic.\- If you need strict per-tenant throughput guarantees (no preemption), we recommend Option B. For Option A we quantify headroom with a 2:1 headroom ratio (i.e., extra capacity to cover instantaneous 2x spikes before burst throttling).

I've attached a draft SLO and a quick diagram of proposed queueing. Next steps: 1) Vivek and Karthik can confirm implementation constraints, 2) we run a short load test (one week) to validate p95/p99 under your load profile, and 3) we map to a contract clause for credits.

Attachments: Nimbus_SLO_draft_20260804.pdf, queueing_behavior_v1.png

I'll sync internally with infra and pricing and propose a specific test window.

Thanks —
Kimberly Park
Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference

From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>

Date: 2026-08-05T08:23:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated pool throughput and evening spike behavior (implementation notes)

On Wed, Aug 4, 2026 at 1:02 PM Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai> wrote:
> I've attached a draft SLO and a quick diagram of proposed queueing.

Couple of implementation points from infra: 

1) Kernel/runtime: for seq len ~128 we get the most predictable latency using our fused attention path and per-request KV prefetch; tail behavior at high throughput depends heavily on batching width. We'll cap per-GPU concurrent streams and use adaptive batching to keep p95 stable.

2) Headroom token model: we can expose an opt-in "burst credit" meter tied to your reserved pool. Credits accrue from unused baseline capacity over rolling 24h window. Credits burn during bursts; once credits deplete, enrichment jobs enter a preemptible queue with an enqueue timeout (configurable, default 30s).

3) Strict carve-out (Option B) requires a private tenant pool — this prevents opportunistic scheduling and simplifies accounting, but you'll pay for the reserved hardware 24/7. For contract language we should define: guaranteed throughput (tokens/s), measurement window (5m rolling), and credit calc (credit% = (1 - observed/committed) * weight factor).

4) Failover: if dedicated pool becomes unhealthy, we can automatically failover to a compatible hosted model (slower cost path) but latency/throughput will degrade; we should define an MTTR and a fallback SLA in the contract.

I'll support the load test if procurement signs off. We should also run a short synthetic test and a replay of Nimbus' production trace.

—Vivek

From: Sophie Tanner <sophie.tanner@nimbus-analytics.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.ai>
Cc: CloudOps Procurement <procure@cloudops.com>
Date: 2026-08-05T11:46:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated pool throughput and evening spike behavior

Thanks team — this is very helpful. A few clarifications from procurement/legal: 

• Credit formula: we want a deterministic, line-item-friendly formula. If you can propose a sample table (e.g., 0–1% shortfall = 5% credit, 1–5% = 10% credit, >5% = 25% credit) tied to the 5-minute rolling window that would make review quicker.
• Failover SLA: we need the worst-case fallback characteristics in the contract (expected p95 and throughput when failing to hosted fallback). Can you provide numbers or a band?
• Load test: procurement requires a one-week signed test with a simple pass/fail gating based on p95/p99 thresholds and an agreed trace to replay.

If you can draft those three items (credit table, fallback bands, load test plan) and send to procure@cloudops.com we'll start legal review. Doc attached with our procurement checklist.

Best,
Sophie
